content.overview: Section 20 of the Specific Relief Act, 1963, as substituted in 2018, is substituted performance. Where a contract is broken by non-performance, the party who suffers the breach may have the contract performed by a third party or by his own agency, and may recover the expenses and other costs actually incurred, spent or suffered from the party in breach. A written notice of not less than thirty days is required, calling on the party in breach to perform and warning that substituted performance will be obtained if he does not. Once substituted performance is obtained, specific performance is barred. The old section 20 discretion to refuse specific performance is not the present section.
content.study: Count thirty days from the notice before treating substituted performance as available. Recover actual cost, not a penalty. After using this section, do not also seek specific performance.

learningObjectives: State the section 20 option and the thirty-day notice.
Limit recovery to actual expenses and costs.
Record the bar on later specific performance.
enhancement.definition: Section 20 lets the injured party, after at least thirty days' notice, have the broken contract performed by a third party or by his own agency and recover the actual cost.
enhancement.legalPrinciple: Substituted performance is an election. Taking it closes specific performance of that contract.
enhancement.statutoryFramework: Specific Relief Act, 1963, section 20, as amended in 2018. Sections 14(a) and 16(a) are the consequences.
essentialIngredients: Notice of not less than thirty days
Notice requires performance and states the substituted-performance warning
Performance by a third party or the injured party's agency
Recovery of expenses and costs actually incurred, spent or suffered
enhancement.detailedExplanation: The option belongs to the party who suffers the breach. The notice must be in writing and of not less than thirty days. It asks the party in breach to perform within the time specified in the notice, and it must state that, if he does not, the injured party may get the performance done by a third party or by his own agency. The recoverable amount is the expenses and other costs actually incurred, spent or suffered. The section is not a liquidated-damages clause. Subsection (2) of the amended section bars specific performance after substituted performance has been obtained. That is why sections 14 and 16 repeat the bar. The pre-2018 judicial discretion in the old section 20 is not this provision.
examples: The contractor stops. The owner gives a thirty-day notice and then engages another contractor. The actual extra cost is recoverable, and specific performance is barred.
The owner engages another contractor on day ten, with no thirty-day notice. The section 20 condition is not met.
The owner recovers the substituted cost and also sues for a conveyance. Sections 14 and 16 bar the second relief.
enhancement.problemApplication: Check breach, a thirty-day notice with the warning, actual cost, and whether substituted performance was in fact obtained. If it was, refuse specific performance.
distinctions: Actual cost vs damages at large
Present section 20 vs the old refusal discretion
enhancement.caseLawNotes: No new case citation or ratio was added. Ready-and-willing and adequate-relief readings remain on the case-law gate.

keyTakeaways: The trigger is breach by non-performance.
Notice must be at least thirty days.
Performance may be by a third party or the injured party's agency.
Recovery is of actual expenses and costs.
